6060: Favourable means working in someone's benefit, showing approval, or helping something succeed. The easiest way to lock this in is through the phrase "in your favour" — when something is favourable, it is on your side. It supports you, benefits you, or pleases you.

1. Helpful or giving an advantage

When conditions, circumstances, or situations are favourable, they make it easier for something to happen or go well. Nothing is blocking you — everything is lined up to help.

  • "The weather was favourable for sailing."

(The wind and sea were just right — perfect for the activity.)

  • "She got a loan at a favourable interest rate."

(The rate was low and worked to her benefit.)

  • "The timing was favourable."

(The moment was just right for something to happen.)

2. Showing approval or a positive opinion

When someone's reaction, review, or judgment is favourable, it means they like something or think well of it.

  • "The new restaurant received favourable reviews."

(Critics liked it and said good things about it.)

  • "His work made a favourable impression on his boss."

(His boss saw his work and thought highly of him.)

  • "The committee looked upon the proposal favourably."

(The committee approved of it.)

3. Suggesting a good outcome is coming

When signs, early results, or early indications are favourable, they point toward a positive result in the future.

  • "The test results were favourable."

(The results showed something positive.)

  • "Early signs are favourable."

(Things look promising so far.)
The One Idea Behind All Three Senses

Notice something? All three senses share one soul: something is helping, supporting, or approving. Whether it is the weather helping a sailor, a boss approving of an employee's work, or test results pointing toward good health — in every case, something is on your side.

These are the word combinations you will most commonly see "favourable" used in:

  • Favourable conditions — circumstances that make success easier
  • Favourable impression — a good image you leave on someone
  • Favourable response — a positive or approving reaction
  • Favourable review / reception — positive feedback or praise
  • Favourable outcome — a result that goes well
  • Favourable terms — conditions of an agreement that benefit you
  • Favourable light — "to see/show someone in a favourable light" means to think well of them or present them positively
  • Compare favourably — to be seen as good or better when compared to something else ("This hotel compares favourably with far more expensive ones.")

The word can be strengthened or softened:

  • Highly favourable → very positive, very helpful
  • Broadly/generally favourable → positive on the whole, even if not perfect in every detail
  • Reasonably favourable → somewhat helpful or positive, but not overwhelmingly so

The opposite is unfavourable — meaning harmful, disapproving, or not helpful.

  • Unfavourable conditions make things harder.
  • An unfavourable review criticises something.
  • An unfavourable comparison makes something look worse, not better.

• Good is broad and general. Favourable is more precise — it specifically means good for a purpose or good in someone's eyes.
  • Positive is close. But positive simply means "not negative," while favourable carries the added idea of actively helping or supporting something.
  • Beneficial means something gives a clear benefit. Favourable can mean that, but it also covers approval and promising signs — not just direct benefit.
  • Promising suggests a good future outcome. Favourable can do the same, but it is broader — it also covers conditions and opinions, not just future potential.
Whenever you see the word favourable, ask yourself: "Is this working in someone's benefit or showing approval?" If the answer is yes, you have understood it correctly.
6061: Favouritism is the act or practice of giving special, unearned advantages or preferential treatment to a particular person or group, not because they have earned it or deserve it, but simply because of a personal connection, personal liking, or bias toward them. It is a form of unfair partiality.

Think of it this way. Imagine a teacher has 30 students in a class. One of them is her nephew. Even when her nephew submits poor work, she gives him high marks. Even when he misbehaves, she ignores it. Even when a more deserving student should be picked for an award, she picks her nephew. That teacher is showing favouritism.

Notice what is happening: she is not treating people based on what they have done or how they have performed. She is treating them based on who they are to her personally. That gap — the gap between what someone deserves and what they actually receive because of a personal connection — is exactly where favouritism lives.

This is the most important thing to understand. Not all preferential treatment is favouritism. A manager who gives a pay rise to the employee who worked the hardest is showing preference, but it is earned preference — it is fair. Favouritism is specifically the kind of preference that bypasses fairness entirely.

Three conditions are usually present when favouritism is occurring:

There is a position of power or influence involved. Favouritism requires someone who has the ability to give advantages — a boss, a teacher, a judge, a parent, a government official.

The advantage being given is something others could or should also be competing for equally — a job, a promotion, a prize, an opportunity, resources, or protection.

The reason for giving the advantage is personal — a friendship, a family relationship, a shared background, a personal liking — rather than merit, qualification, or fair criteria.

When all three are present, you have favouritism.
Where Favouritism Appears in Real Life

Favouritism is not confined to one setting. It can appear almost anywhere there is power and relationships coexisting.

In the workplace, a manager might hire a friend who is less qualified than other candidates, or give a cousin a promotion they did not earn, or assign the best projects only to people they personally like. Other employees are left at a disadvantage through no fault of their own.

In schools and universities, a teacher or professor might grade a favourite student more generously, overlook their rule-breaking, or pick them for opportunities regardless of ability. Other students who work just as hard or harder are passed over.

In families, a parent might consistently favour one child over others — giving them more freedom, more resources, more praise, or more support, not based on need or circumstance, but simply out of personal preference. This is sometimes called playing favourites.

In government and politics, favouritism takes the form of politicians awarding contracts, positions, or public resources to allies, donors, or friends rather than to whoever is most qualified or most deserving. This overlaps closely with corruption.

In sports, a referee or judge might make decisions that consistently benefit a particular player or team because of personal bias, not based on what actually happened in the game.

In social groups, a person in a leadership role — say, a club president or a community organiser — might distribute responsibilities, recognition, or benefits to people they are close to, while equally capable people on the outside of that inner circle are overlooked.

People do not always show favouritism out of malicious intent. Often, it is driven by deeply natural human tendencies that, when left unchecked, become unfair.

Human beings are naturally more comfortable with, and more trusting of, people who are similar to them, familiar to them, or personally close to them. This is a psychological tendency sometimes called in-group bias. We instinctively want to help the people we like and care about.

In many cases, favouritism is not even conscious. A manager might genuinely believe they are choosing the best candidate, when in reality their liking for that person is subtly colouring their judgement. This unconscious form is sometimes harder to address than the deliberate kind.

Other times, favouritism is entirely deliberate — a person knows exactly what they are doing and chooses to prioritise their personal relationships over fairness because it benefits them, their family, or their social circle.

Favouritism causes real harm, and understanding those harms helps explain why it is considered a serious flaw in any system, relationship, or institution.

It creates deep resentment and a sense of injustice among those who are treated less favourably. When people see that outcomes are determined not by effort or ability but by personal connections, they feel that their contributions are worthless — because in that context, they are.

It damages the overall quality of outcomes. When the best person for a job, a role, or a prize is routinely passed over in favour of someone's personal favourite, the results are worse for everyone. Organisations that run on favouritism tend to perform poorly because they are not putting their best people in their best positions.

It erodes trust. Once people recognise that a system is driven by favouritism, they lose faith in it. A court where judges show favouritism is not a court anyone can trust. A school where teachers show favouritism is not a place where students can feel they will be judged fairly.

It reinforces inequality. Favouritism tends to perpetuate advantage for those who are already connected, already in the inner circle, already close to power — and it keeps disadvantaged people further out.
Favouritism vs. Fair Preference — An Important Distinction

It is worth being clear on this, because the line can sometimes seem blurry.

Choosing the most qualified candidate for a job is not favouritism — it is fair selection. Giving a prize to the student with the best essay is not favouritism — it is merit-based reward. Even choosing to spend more time helping someone who is genuinely struggling more than others is not favouritism — it is a reasonable, justified response to a real difference in need.

Favouritism only occurs when the preferential treatment is not justified by any fair, reasonable, or objective standard. The moment personal connection overrides fair criteria, favouritism begins.

Similarly, having personal opinions and preferences about people is entirely human and not inherently wrong. The problem arises when a person in a position of power or influence allows those personal preferences to distort decisions that should be based on something more objective — merit, need, qualification, or fairness.

Nepotism is a specific, named form of favouritism that refers exclusively to favouring family members — giving jobs, positions, or advantages to relatives simply because they are relatives, regardless of their ability.

Cronyism is another specific form in which a person in power favours their close friends or allies — often in professional or political contexts — over more qualified or deserving candidates.

Both nepotism and cronyism are types of favouritism, but favouritism itself is the broader, more general term that covers all forms of unjust preferential treatment, regardless of whether the person being favoured is a family member, a friend, or simply someone the powerful person likes.

Bias is a related but slightly different concept. Bias refers to a leaning or tendency toward or against something. Favouritism can be the result of bias — particularly unconscious bias — but bias does not always lead to favouritism. You can hold a bias internally without it affecting your decisions. Favouritism is when bias (or simple personal preference) actually changes how you treat people.

Favouritism, in its simplest form, is this: treating someone better than others not because they deserve it, but because you personally like them, know them, or are connected to them. It is preference without justification — partiality without fairness. It appears in workplaces, schools, families, governments, and social groups. It causes resentment, damages quality, erodes trust, and deepens inequality. It is driven by natural human instincts that, when unchecked by fairness and accountability, turn into a practice that is widely regarded as unjust. Its close relatives are nepotism (favouring family) and cronyism (favouring allies), but favouritism itself is the overarching term for all such unjustified preferential treatment.
6062: Fawn has two meanings as a noun — one about an animal, one about a color. Both are common and worth knowing well.

A fawn is a baby deer, specifically one that is less than one year old. Once it turns a year old, it is no longer called a fawn — it becomes a "yearling." So "fawn" is a very age-specific word.

What does a fawn look like?
A fawn is small, delicate, and wobbly on its legs. Its most distinctive feature is its coat: a reddish-brown or tan background covered in white spots. These spots are not just decorative — they serve as camouflage, making the fawn blend in with sunlit patches of forest floor. As the fawn grows older, these spots slowly disappear.

Fawns are born knowing how to walk, but they are still extremely vulnerable in their first weeks. Their mothers often leave them hidden in tall grass or bushes for hours at a time while she goes to feed. This is normal and not abandonment — a doe (mother deer) knows that her scent attracts predators, so she stays away to keep her fawn safe. The fawn instinctively stays still and quiet.

Which animals are called fawns?
The word fawn primarily refers to the young of deer (like white-tailed deer, red deer, or roe deer). It is also sometimes used for the young of closely related animals like antelopes. For most other animals, different words are used — a baby horse is a foal, a baby cow is a calf, and so on.

Example sentences:

  • "A fawn was curled up beneath the oak tree, barely visible in the dry leaves."
  • "The mother deer nudged the fawn gently to get it to stand."
  • "We spotted a fawn at the edge of the forest, still young enough to have its white spots."

Fawn is also the name of a color — a soft, warm, pale beige-brown, like the color of a young deer's coat. It sits somewhere between tan and light brown, with a slightly golden or sandy warmth to it. It is not quite white, not quite yellow, and not quite brown — it is a gentle, neutral, earthy tone.

This color is widely used in fashion, interior design, and art. A "fawn coat" or "fawn-colored walls" immediately tells you the shade without needing further explanation. It is a softer, warmer alternative to grey or plain beige.

Example sentences:

  • "She wore a fawn sweater that matched her leather bag perfectly."
  • "The room was painted in fawn, giving it a calm, cozy feel."
  • "The puppy had a fawn coat with a white patch on its chest."
How the Two Meanings Are Connected

These two meanings are not separate accidents — the color is named after the animal. The pale brownish-yellow of a baby deer's fur is exactly what gave the color its name. When you know this, both meanings become easy to remember together.

What it means
Animal senseA baby deer (under one year old), known for its spotted coat
Color senseA soft, warm, pale brownish-yellow — the color of a deer's fur

If someone uses "fawn" and you are unsure which meaning they intend, context almost always makes it clear: a fawn hiding in the grass is the animal; fawn-colored furniture is the color.
6063:
To fawn means to try to win someone's approval or favor by showering them with excessive praise, acting extremely submissive, and being overly eager to please — in a way that feels exaggerated, undignified, and driven by self-interest rather than genuine feeling.

Think of it this way: when you honestly compliment a friend, that's normal and sincere. But when someone continuously heaps exaggerated praise on a powerful person, agrees with everything they say, and behaves almost like a servant just to gain something in return — that is fawning.

When describing human behavior (the most common use), fawning involves praising someone far more than they deserve, agreeing with them even when you privately disagree, hanging on their every word with theatrical attentiveness, and doing all of this with a hidden motive — to gain favor, a promotion, money, protection, or simply to avoid conflict with someone who has power over you.

"The interns fawned over the manager, laughing loudly at his jokes and praising his every idea."

The interns here aren't just being polite. They're being excessive, probably insincere, and their real goal is to make the manager like them or treat them favorably.

When describing animal behavior (particularly dogs), fawning is a physical display of affection and submission — tail-wagging, jumping up, licking, crouching low. In this case, the behavior is innocent and genuine, not manipulative at all.

"The puppy fawned on the child the moment she arrived."

This animal meaning is actually the older, more literal use of the word. The human meaning grew out of it — the idea being that a person who fawns is behaving like an overly excited, tail-wagging animal desperate for approval.
Why Fawning Is Always a Negative Word (When Used About People)

This is crucial to understand: when applied to a person, fawn always carries a negative connotation. No one says "she fawned over her professor" as a compliment. It implies that the behavior is excessive and beyond what's normal, that the person is acting without self-respect or dignity, that the flattery is dishonest and self-serving, and that it makes the person doing it look weak, desperate, or hollow.

If someone calls you a "fawner," they are insulting you — saying you're a people-pleaser who demeans yourself to win approval from those above you.
What Separates Fawning From Similar Behaviors

This is where many learners get confused, so let's draw clear lines.

Genuine admiration vs. fawning: If you truly respect someone and tell them so honestly, that is not fawning. Fawning is when the praise is clearly exaggerated or driven by a hidden agenda, not by honest feeling.

Politeness vs. fawning: Being respectful and courteous to your boss is normal social behavior. Telling him he's a genius five times a day hoping to get a raise — that's fawning.

Flattery vs. fawning: Flattery is a single act — one exaggerated compliment. Fawning is a sustained pattern of submissive, eager-to-please behavior. It's flattery turned into a whole way of conducting yourself around someone powerful.

You'll most often see fawn paired with "over" in modern usage:

"She fawns over her boss." / "The crowd fawned over the celebrity."

The older, more formal pairing is "on", meaning exactly the same thing:

"The courtiers fawned on the king."

Both are correct. "Fawn over" is what you'll encounter most often today.

• "He fawned over the investor, calling him visionary and brilliant, hoping to receive funding."
  • "She hated how her colleagues fawned over the director the moment he entered the room."
  • "The politician's supporters fawned over him at every rally, treating him as though he could do no wrong."
  • "Stop fawning — I don't need your flattery, just your honest opinion."

Fawning (adjective) — describing behavior that is fawn-like: "His fawning attitude toward management irritated everyone around him."

Fawningly (adverb) — in a fawning manner: "She smiled fawningly and agreed with everything he said."

Fawner (noun) — a person who fawns: "He was a well-known fawner who never disagreed with anyone in authority."

Knowing the family of words around "fawn" will help you understand exactly where it sits:

Toady — to flatter and agree with someone purely for personal gain. Very close to fawning. A "toady" is also a noun for such a person.

Grovel — to behave in an extremely submissive way, often in response to someone's anger or power. More desperate and humiliating than fawning.

Kowtow — to be excessively submissive to someone. Often used in a political or social power context.

Bootlick — an informal and more colorful word for fawning. Very direct and slightly crude.

Ingratiate (oneself) — to make yourself popular with someone through flattering or overly pleasing behavior. More neutral in tone than fawning, but carries a similar implication of insincerity.

Among all of these, "fawn" is special because it evokes a vivid physical image — the crouching, tail-wagging, eager-eyed animal desperately seeking approval. That image is exactly what the word is meant to conjure when describing a person. It's both precise and slightly humiliating, which is why it stings when used about someone.

In contemporary psychology, "fawning" has taken on a more specific and serious meaning as a trauma response. Alongside the well-known fight, flight, and freeze responses, psychologists now recognize a fourth: the fawn response, where a person instinctively appeases, flatters, or complies with someone threatening in order to avoid conflict or harm. People who grew up in difficult or abusive environments sometimes develop automatic fawning behavior as a survival mechanism. This is a deeper, clinical layer of the word you may encounter if you read psychology or self-help literature.

To fawn is to pour excessive, often insincere flattery and eager submission onto someone — usually someone with power — in order to gain their favor, and it is always seen as a sign of lacking dignity or honesty.
6064:
When someone is fawning, they are showing excessive, over-the-top admiration or flattery toward someone — usually to impress them, please them, or gain something from them. The behavior feels hollow and insincere because the goal isn't genuine appreciation; it's self-serving.

Think of it this way: there's a difference between a person who genuinely tells their boss, "That was a great idea," because it truly was, and a person who tells their boss "Oh, that's absolutely brilliant! You're so smart! Everything you say is gold!" — even when the idea is mediocre. The second person is being fawning.

A fawning person:

  • Praises excessively and insincerely — far more than the situation deserves
  • Acts overly submissive — almost like they're bowing down emotionally
  • Does it with a motive — to win approval, avoid conflict, get a reward, or stay in someone's good books
  • Abandons their own honest opinion — they say what the other person wants to hear, not what is true

The key ingredient that makes something "fawning" is that it goes beyond what is genuine. A little honest compliment is kindness. A flood of empty, calculated praise is fawning.

Fawning almost always happens when there is a gap in power or status. The fawning person is usually in a lower or weaker position and is trying to please someone above them:

  • An employee fawning over a boss
  • A student fawning over a professor
  • A politician fawning over a more powerful leader
  • A celebrity's fan fawning over them in a desperate, clingy way

However, it can also happen between equals — for example, someone fawning over a popular person at school to be accepted.
The Tone: It Is Always Negative

This is important — "fawning" is never a compliment. When you describe someone's behavior as fawning, you are criticizing it. It implies:

  • A lack of dignity — the person seems desperate
  • A lack of honesty — the praise is hollow
  • A lack of backbone — they won't say anything real or critical

If someone calls a news article a "fawning interview," they mean the journalist asked only soft, flattering questions and never challenged the subject — which is bad journalism. If someone says a colleague is "fawning" over the manager, they mean the colleague is being fake and desperate.

1. In the workplace:
An employee who laughs loudly at every single joke the CEO makes — even unfunny ones — rushes to agree with every opinion the CEO expresses, and constantly volunteers compliments like "What a visionary you are!" is being fawning. Everyone around them can usually see through it.

2. In the media:
A reporter who interviews a famous actor and only asks questions like "You're so talented — how does it feel to be so loved?" without asking anything challenging or real is writing a fawning piece.

3. In everyday life:
Imagine someone who wants to borrow money from a rich relative. Suddenly, they start calling them the "wisest, most generous, most wonderful person" they know. That sudden overflow of excessive praise is fawning.
What Fawning Looks Like in Practice

Fawning behavior typically involves some combination of:

  • Constant agreement — never disagreeing, always nodding along
  • Exaggerated compliments — praising ordinary things as if they were extraordinary
  • Eager helpfulness — rushing to do favors, often without being asked, to impress
  • Laughing at bad jokes — finding everything the powerful person says funny or clever
  • Avoiding any criticism — even when it would be honest and helpful
A Simple Test to Recognize Fawning

Ask yourself: "Is this praise genuine and proportionate, or is it excessive and calculated?"

  • Genuine praise = honest, measured, and given because it's deserved
  • Fawning praise = inflated, constant, and driven by a hidden personal goal

If the admiration seems more about the admirer's needs than about the person being praised, it's very likely fawning.

Understanding these related words will sharpen your grasp of "fawning":

  • Sycophantic — almost identical in meaning; a sycophant is a classic "yes-man" who flatters to gain favor
  • Obsequious — excessively eager to serve or please, in an uncomfortable, groveling way
  • Flattering — can be neutral or mildly positive on its own, but when overdone and insincere, it tips into fawning territory
  • Groveling — even more extreme; almost begging in a self-degrading way

"Fawning" sits comfortably in this family of words. It's less about begging (that's groveling) and more about excessive, insincere admiration used as a social tool.

Fawning = behavior that is overly complimentary, submissive, and eager to please — not out of genuine feeling, but out of a desire to win favor, approval, or advantage. It's always seen negatively, because it involves a sacrifice of honesty and self-respect in exchange for social or personal gain. When you see someone heaping far more praise on a person than they deserve — especially a person in power — and you sense it has an ulterior motive, that's fawning.
6065:
To faze someone means to disturb, unsettle, or bother them emotionally or mentally — to make them feel rattled, thrown off, or no longer calm and composed.

When something fazes you, it gets to you. It shakes your confidence, makes you anxious, or leaves you flustered. The disturbance is internal — it affects your mind, your mood, or your sense of being in control.

Typically, it's something challenging, threatening, surprising, or overwhelming — something that most people would find hard to face without feeling some inner disruption.

  • A terrifying experience
  • Harsh criticism or insults
  • Enormous pressure or high stakes
  • Shocking or upsetting news
  • A hostile crowd, a difficult confrontation, a rude person
The Key Nuance: Degree of Reaction

"Faze" doesn't imply total breakdown or panic. It captures a moderate inner disturbance — a wobble in your composure. Think of it as the feeling of being mentally or emotionally knocked slightly off-balance.

Here's the most important thing to know: faze almost always appears in the negative. People use it to say that something did not disturb someone — to express that a person remained calm and unaffected in the face of something difficult.

"Nothing fazes her." — She stays completely calm no matter what happens.

"The hostile crowd didn't faze him one bit." — He was not rattled or intimidated by them at all.

"She walked into the burning building, completely unfazed." — She showed no sign of fear or disturbance.

You'll hear "unfazed" very often — it means a person was not affected, not shaken, not disturbed. It's a quiet compliment to someone's composure and nerve.

That said, it can also be used positively (to say something did faze someone):

"The unexpected question fazed him for a moment." — It unsettled him briefly; he didn't know how to respond right away.

"Losing his job fared— fazed him deeply." — It shook him, made him anxious and uncertain.

• A soldier who has seen many battles is described as unfazed by gunfire — it no longer disturbs his composure.
  • A student who barely studied is fazed when they see how hard the exam is — they're visibly rattled and anxious.
  • A veteran surgeon stays unfazed during a difficult, high-pressure operation — she doesn't lose her calm.
  • A young actor is fazed by the sudden fame — all the attention and pressure disturbs his sense of normalcy.
  • A mountain climber is asked if the dangerous heights faze her. She says, "Not at all."

Many people — even native speakers — incorrectly write "phase" when they mean "faze." These are two completely different words.

  • Faze (verb) = to disturb or unsettle someone emotionally. "Nothing fazes him."
  • Phase (noun/verb) = a stage or period, or to introduce/remove something gradually. "We're in the planning phase." / "They phased out the old system."

So the correct sentence is: "It didn't faze me" — not "It didn't phase me."

This is one of the most common spelling errors in English. Knowing this will serve you well.
To faze someone is to disturb their inner calm — to unsettle, rattle, or throw them off mentally or emotionally, even if only briefly.
6066: Fealty means a deep, solemn, and binding loyalty that a person pledges to someone or something that holds authority over them. It is not casual loyalty — it is the kind that comes with a sense of duty and obligation. When you swear fealty to someone, you are making a serious, formal promise to be faithful and serve them.

Think of fealty as loyalty with weight behind it. Ordinary loyalty can be informal — you can be loyal to a friend simply because you care about them. Fealty is different. It carries a sense of commitment, duty, and often, a sworn promise. It answers the question: "To whom do you belong, and who can count on you no matter what?"

There are three things always present in the idea of fealty:

  1. A pledge — It is not just a feeling. Fealty is something you declare, swear, or formally commit to.
  2. A power relationship — Fealty flows upward. You give fealty to someone above you in rank, authority, or importance — a leader, a ruler, an institution, or a cause you serve.
  3. An ongoing obligation — It is not a one-time act. Swearing fealty means you are bound to that loyalty continuously, not just when it is convenient.
Where This Word Comes From in Practice

Historically, fealty was used in the context of medieval kingdoms. A knight or a lord of lower rank would kneel before a king and formally swear an oath — promising to be faithful, to not betray them, and to serve them loyally. In return, the king might grant them land or protection. This oath was called an oath of fealty, and breaking it was considered one of the worst acts of betrayal imaginable. The word carries that gravity even today.

While fealty was born in the world of kings and knights, people use it today in much broader and often figurative ways. You will find it used in:

  • Politics: "The senator showed complete fealty to the party, never voting against its wishes."
  • Religion or ideology: "Her fealty to her faith never wavered, even in the hardest times."
  • Business or organizations: "He expected fealty from every member of his team."
  • Values or principles: "His fealty to the truth made him refuse to sign the misleading report."

In every case, the word signals that this is not light loyalty — it is deep, serious, and binding.

• "Swear fealty" — to make a formal pledge of loyalty. "The soldiers swore fealty to the new commander."
  • "Pledge fealty" — same meaning, slightly more modern. "She pledged fealty to the cause."
  • "Owe fealty" — to be obligated to remain loyal. "As a vassal, he owed fealty to the king."
  • "Demand fealty" — when someone in power requires loyalty from those under them. "The dictator demanded fealty from every official in his government."
  • "Fealty to [person/thing]" — describing who or what the loyalty is directed toward. "His fealty to the constitution was unshakeable."
How Fealty Differs from Similar Words

These words are close cousins, but they are not the same:

Loyalty is the broadest of these words. You can be loyal to a friend, a sports team, or a brand. It does not need to be formal or involve a power difference.

Allegiance is closer to fealty but tends to be used for loyalty to a country, government, or cause. "I pledge allegiance to the flag" is the classic example. Allegiance is formal but not always sworn personally to an individual.

Fidelity means faithfulness, particularly in the sense of not straying or betraying. It is commonly used in romantic contexts ("fidelity in a marriage") but can be used more broadly.

Fealty is the most solemn and formal of all these. It always implies a pledge, always involves a power relationship, and always carries a sense of deep obligation. If loyalty is a feeling, fealty is a vow.

Fealty is not everyday language. It is a formal, elevated word. When a writer or speaker uses it, they are deliberately signaling seriousness. If a journalist writes "the cabinet members showed complete fealty to the president," they are painting a picture of absolute, unquestioning loyalty — the kind where no one dares to speak against the leader. The word often carries a slightly critical or cautionary undertone in modern usage, suggesting that the loyalty being described might be excessive or blind.

Fealty = a solemn, sworn, binding loyalty given to a person or cause that holds authority over you, carrying a strong sense of duty and obligation. It is deeper than ordinary loyalty, more formal than allegiance, and always implies that you have committed yourself — your actions and faithfulness — to someone or something above you.
6067:
Something fearsome is so powerful, dangerous, or overwhelming that it makes you feel afraid — or at least deeply intimidated. When you call something fearsome, you are saying it has a quality that strikes fear into people. It isn't just a little scary. It is impressively, strikingly scary — the kind of thing that stops you in your tracks.

The fearsome lion let out a roar that silenced the entire jungle.

"Fearsome" carries two closely related meanings, and understanding both will give you a complete picture of the word.

Shade 1 — Literally frightening: Something that genuinely makes people afraid. This is the most direct meaning. A fearsome creature, a fearsome storm, or a fearsome weapon — these things pose a real sense of danger or threat.

The soldiers had never faced such a fearsome enemy — one who seemed to feel no pain at all.

The fearsome tornado tore through the town in minutes.

Shade 2 — Impressively powerful or intense: Here, "fearsome" is used to describe something that is so remarkable in its power, skill, or scale that it overwhelms or intimidates people — even if there is no literal physical danger. This shade of the word is about awe and intimidation, not just raw terror.

She had a fearsome intellect — her arguments were so sharp that nobody dared challenge her in a debate.

The team has built a fearsome reputation over the years.

In this second use, people aren't running away in panic, but they are still deeply unsettled or daunted by the sheer force of what they're dealing with.

Here is an important insight: fearsome combines two feelings — fear and a kind of grudging awe.

Something fearsome doesn't just make you want to run. It also commands a certain respect or amazement. You look at it and think, "That is extraordinary — and terrifying." This is why the word is often used to describe great warriors, fierce animals, or remarkably powerful forces of nature. There's almost something impressive about a fearsome thing, even as it scares you.

This is subtly different from something being simply ugly, unpleasant, or uncomfortable — a fearsome thing has power. It earns its fear.

"Fearsome" is a fairly strong and dramatic word. It isn't what you'd use for something mildly worrying. You wouldn't say the slightly cold weather outside is fearsome, or that a wasp buzzing near you is fearsome. The word is reserved for things that are genuinely formidable in scale, strength, or intensity.

Think of it on a scale:
Unsettling → Scary → Frightening → Fearsome → Terrifying

"Fearsome" sits toward the stronger end of this scale. It is intense, but it doesn't necessarily mean total panic-inducing terror — that's closer to terrifying. Fearsome is about being powerful enough to inspire deep fear or serious intimidation.

Frightening is the most general word — it just means something scares you. "Fearsome" is more specific and dramatic; it adds the sense of being impressively powerful.

Formidable means something that is very difficult to deal with or compete against. It's similar to the second shade of "fearsome," but formidable doesn't carry fear as directly — it's more about being a tough challenge. Fearsome has a stronger emotional punch.

Terrifying is more extreme. It suggests full-blown, overwhelming terror. "Fearsome" is powerful but a little more controlled — it can describe something you are in awe of, not just something that makes you lose your mind with fear.

Daunting means something that makes you feel hesitant or puts you off trying. It's milder and more about discouragement than fear. "Fearsome" is heavier and more dramatic than daunting.

To help you picture the word naturally, here are the kinds of things people typically describe as fearsome:

  • Animals and creatures: a fearsome predator, a fearsome beast, a fearsome shark
  • People: a fearsome warrior, a fearsome opponent, a fearsome ruler
  • Skills and abilities: a fearsome intellect, a fearsome talent, a fearsome serve (in tennis)
  • Reputation or power: a fearsome reputation, a fearsome force, a fearsome army
  • Natural forces: a fearsome storm, a fearsome blaze, a fearsome hurricane
  • Tasks or challenges: a fearsome task, a fearsome ordeal

Here are several sentences across different contexts to show you how naturally the word works:

  • The dragon was a fearsome creature, with scales like iron and breath like a furnace.
  • He was known as a fearsome negotiator — nobody ever walked away from the table feeling they had won.
  • The climbers stood at the base of the fearsome mountain, wondering if they had made a terrible mistake.
  • The school's debate team had a fearsome reputation that scared off other schools from even entering the competition.
  • The storm unleashed fearsome winds that uprooted trees and flattened fences.
  • Despite her small frame, she was a fearsome competitor who had never lost a match.

• It is not a word for something merely unpleasant or annoying — bad traffic is not fearsome.
  • It is not weak or mild in tone — it is a word with weight and drama.
  • It does not have to mean something is evil or bad. A fearsome intellect is an extraordinary thing — admirable, even. The "fear" in fearsome is about being overwhelmed, not about something being wicked.

Fearsome means: so powerful, dangerous, or impressive that it fills people with fear or deep awe — whether that's a roaring predator, a devastating storm, or a mind so sharp it leaves everyone around it at a loss.
6068:
Feasibility is a noun that refers to how possible, practical, and achievable something is — given the real-world conditions, resources, and constraints that actually exist.

When you ask "Is this feasible?", you are not just asking "Can this happen in theory?" You are asking something much more grounded and practical: "Can this actually be done — by real people, with the time, money, skills, and tools we actually have?"

Think of feasibility as a measure of real-world doability. It sits at the intersection of "Is this possible?" and "Is this realistic?"

Here is the key insight that unlocks the word:

Something can be possible without being feasible.

For example:

  • It is possible for a small village to build a space rocket. But is it feasible? No — they don't have the engineers, the funding, the materials, or the technology.
  • It is possible for a student to read 1,000 books in a month. But is it feasible? No — there simply isn't enough time.

Feasibility is what bridges the gap between imagination and reality. It asks: "Yes, but can WE actually do THIS, HERE, NOW?"

The feasibility of something is judged across several real-world dimensions. These aren't separate meanings of the word — they are all part of what the single word captures when used in context:

1. Physical / Technical feasibility — Can it actually be built or done with existing technology and human capability? Building a bridge across a small river is feasible. Building a bridge across an ocean is not — at least not yet.

2. Financial feasibility — Do we have enough money to do it? Can it be afforded? A family might want to buy a mansion, but the financial feasibility of that plan depends entirely on their income and savings.

3. Time feasibility — Can it be done within the available time? Finishing a 300-page novel in one night has very low feasibility.

4. Legal / Regulatory feasibility — Is it allowed? Even if you can physically and financially do something, laws or regulations might make it infeasible.

5. Operational feasibility — Do the people involved have the skills, tools, and systems to actually carry it out smoothly?

When someone uses the word "feasibility" in conversation or writing, they may be referring to one or all of these dimensions — context will tell you which.
How It Is Used in Real Life

The word feasibility appears most often in professional, academic, and planning contexts — anytime people are carefully evaluating whether a plan should move forward.

Common phrases you will encounter:

  • "The feasibility of the project" — meaning whether the project can realistically be completed.
  • "Feasibility study" — a formal investigation carried out before starting a project, specifically designed to check whether the project is realistic and worth pursuing. Businesses, governments, and organizations do these all the time before committing large amounts of money or effort.
  • "Feasibility analysis" — similar to a feasibility study; an evaluation of how workable a plan is.
  • "Questions of feasibility" — doubts or concerns about whether something can actually be done.
  • "Doubtful/questionable feasibility" — suggesting that something is unlikely to be achievable.
  • "Technical feasibility", "financial feasibility", "economic feasibility" — these narrow the word to one specific dimension.

Feasibility is not a simple yes-or-no quality. It exists on a spectrum.

  • Something has high feasibility when it is very realistic and achievable with the available resources.
  • Something has low feasibility when it would be extremely difficult, costly, or impractical — even if not completely impossible.
  • Something has no feasibility when it simply cannot be done under the given conditions.

This is important because the word is often used in discussions where people are weighing options and trying to find the most feasible path forward, not just ruling things out entirely.

It helps to understand feasibility clearly by comparing it to nearby concepts:

  • Possibility is broader and more abstract. "Is it possible?" asks whether something could ever happen under any conditions. "Is it feasible?" asks whether it can happen under these specific, real conditions.
  • Viability is closely related and often used interchangeably, but viability leans more toward long-term sustainability (especially in business — "Is this business viable?" means "Can it survive and succeed over time?"). Feasibility focuses more on whether you can do it in the first place.
  • Practicality is the everyday cousin of feasibility. Feasibility is the more formal, technical term used in planning and analysis. Practicality is the more casual way of asking the same question.
Everyday Examples to Cement Your Understanding

• A city government is thinking about building a new subway line. Before spending billions, they commission a feasibility study to check whether the soil conditions, costs, ridership demand, and legal requirements make the project realistic.
  • A student wants to complete a university degree while working two full-time jobs simultaneously. Her advisor questions the feasibility of this plan, given the limited time and energy she would have for studying.
  • A startup has a brilliant product idea. Investors don't just ask "Is the idea good?" — they ask about feasibility: Can it actually be manufactured at scale? Can it be done within a reasonable budget? Is there a real market for it?
  • A doctor and a patient discuss the feasibility of a new treatment plan, considering the patient's age, health condition, and ability to follow the required routine.
The Underlying Spirit of the Word

Feasibility is a word about honest, grounded thinking. It is what you invoke when you want to move beyond wishful thinking and test an idea against the hard constraints of the real world — time, money, skill, technology, and circumstance.

It is the word that separates dreamers from planners, and good plans from failed ones.

Whenever you see or hear feasibility, ask yourself: "Someone is checking whether this can actually be done in the real world — not just in theory, but truly, practically, and realistically." That instinct will never mislead you.
6069:
Feasible means able to be done successfully in the real world, given the actual conditions.

When you call something feasible, you are saying: "This can actually work. It's not just a dream — it's achievable."

It answers a very practical question: Can this really be done? Not in a perfect world, but in this world, with the time, money, resources, and conditions available.

This is the most important thing to understand about "feasible," and most learners miss it.

"Possible" is a very broad word. It simply means something can happen — it's not impossible. But it doesn't tell you anything about whether it's realistic or practical.

"Feasible" goes a step further. It means something is not only possible, but also workable in practice — realistic given the real circumstances.

Here's an example to feel the difference:

Climbing Mount Everest alone, without oxygen, in winter, in three days — is it possible? Technically, maybe. Is it feasible? Absolutely not. The conditions make it completely impractical.

So think of it this way:

  • Possible = It could happen. (Theory)
  • Feasible = It can realistically be done. (Practice)

Every feasible thing is possible. But not every possible thing is feasible.

Feasible does not mean:

  • Easy. Something can be feasible but still very difficult. A plan can be feasible and still require a lot of hard work and planning.
  • Likely or probable. Feasible means "it can be done," not "it will happen." These are different ideas.
  • The best option. Calling something feasible doesn't mean it's a good idea — just that it's achievable.

Something becomes not feasible (infeasible) when real-world constraints get in the way:

  • Time — "We can't build a hospital in two weeks. It's not feasible."
  • Money/Budget — "Buying a private jet on a student budget isn't feasible."
  • Resources — "Running the factory without electricity is not feasible."
  • Technology or skill — "Curing that disease right now isn't feasible — the science isn't there yet."
  • Physical or logical limits — "It's not feasible to drive from New York to London."

Feasibility isn't always black and white. You'll often see qualifiers used with it:

  • Technically feasible — The technology or method exists to do it, but other factors (like cost) may still be a problem.
  • Economically feasible — The cost is acceptable and realistic.
  • Barely feasible — It's possible, but just barely, under tight conditions.
  • Perfectly / entirely feasible — There's no real obstacle. It can easily be done.

"Feasible" is a moderately formal word. You'll hear it most in:

  • Professional settings ("Is this project plan feasible?")
  • Academic or scientific writing ("The experiment was found to be technically feasible.")
  • Planning and business conversations ("Let's explore all feasible options.")

In casual everyday speech, people often replace it with words like doable or realistic. But "feasible" carries a sharper, more precise meaning than either of those.
Words Close in Meaning (and How They Differ)

WordHow it differs from feasible
PossibleBroader — just means "not impossible," with no judgment about practicality
DoableInformal version of feasible; more casual, less precise
PracticalFocuses on being sensible and convenient, not just achievable
ViableVery similar to feasible, but often implies long-term success too (e.g., a viable business model)
AchievableEmphasizes that a goal can be reached, often with effort
WorkableMeans a plan or system can actually function; focuses on whether it works

The closest synonym is viable, but even there, "viable" often suggests something that can sustain itself over time, while "feasible" is more about whether it can be done at all.

• Infeasible / Not feasible — cannot realistically be done
  • Impossible — cannot be done at all
  • Impractical — too difficult, costly, or complicated to be worth doing
  • Unworkable — the plan or idea simply won't function

Here are examples across different contexts so you can see how naturally the word fits in:

  1. "The engineers confirmed that the new bridge design is feasible within the current budget."
  2. "It's not feasible to expect all employees to work 16-hour days."
  3. "The doctor suggested a few feasible treatment options based on her condition."
  4. "We need to find a feasible solution before the deadline."
  5. "Traveling by boat would take three weeks — it's technically feasible, but completely impractical."
  6. "The government asked scientists whether a carbon-neutral economy was feasible by 2050."
  7. "With the right team and funding, the startup idea is entirely feasible."
Feasible means something can realistically and practically be done, given the real conditions, constraints, and resources available — not just in theory, but in the actual world.
